claims.claim: The hydrator design says the git push secret should live in a namespace separate from the other Argo CD components, but the signing-key design puts the GPG key Secret in the same namespace the rest of the control plane runs in and makes it one cluster-wide key. Any workload already permitted to read Secrets in that namespace (any Argo CD component or extension, not just the commit server) can read the key and mint commits that satisfy the hydrated branch's SourceIntegrity policy, which the application controller then syncs from syncSource.targetBranch to every cluster the hydrated branch feeds. The blast radius of one Secret read is therefore every hydrator-enabled Application in the fleet, and no check between the git host and the cluster distinguishes such a commit from a real hydration.

Server-Side Diff runs as the cluster credential from the cluster Secret and, because Kubernetes RBAC has no dry-run verb, requires real patch authority on every resource kind an Application ships, growing by one kind per new chart with no end state. That reassembles on the standing cluster credential exactly the concentration of privilege the impersonation proposal exists to remove: its stated premise is that the control plane must otherwise be granted the highest privilege any tenant needs, creating a large attack surface where compromising Argo CD yields cluster-wide write. Enabling destinationServiceAccounts does not shrink it, since the diff path ignores that mapping, so whoever obtains the cluster Secret holds write authority on every kind in the external cluster, protected only by Argo CD's convention of sending dryRun=All rather than by any enforced boundary.

The proposed fix for the namespace-label escape is to have the Argo CD control-plane service account handle namespace bootstrapping while the impersonated service account handles the sync, with kind: Namespace removed from the impersonated identity. The impersonation design forecloses that split: it fixes the service account per Application, not per resource, stating that the value in Application.spec.destination.namespace determines the single service account used for all resources present in the Application. So the identity that must be able to create the namespace under CreateNamespace=true is the same identity that applies a Namespace object a tenant commits to the repository, and the pod-security.kubernetes.io/enforce label can still be dropped by a tenant whose namespace name matches the AppProject clusterResourceWhitelist pattern.

The roadmap's multi-tenancy direction is for end users to create Argo CD Applications through Kubernetes directly, without going through the Argo CD API. Combined with the impersonation rule that an Application omitting the optional spec.destination.namespace has its service account scoped to the Application's own namespace (argocd), a tenant who simply leaves that field out gets a sync performed as system:serviceaccount:argocd:<name> in the control-plane namespace, resolved through the catch-all destinationServiceAccounts entry with namespace '*' and defaultServiceAccount default when no narrower entry matches. The field whose omission selects a control-plane-namespace identity is written by the tenant, and nothing in the AppProject destination matching requires it to be set.

The platform call recorded impersonation rollout as a per-project flag, explicitly not fleet-wide, with no project flipped until the diff story is fixed. The impersonation design states the feature can be enabled or disabled only at the system level and that once set it applies to all Argo CD Applications, and that when no service account is named in the matching AppProject the default service account of the destination namespace is used. There is no per-project switch to honor the decision, so acting on it flips the sync identity for every Application in the instance at once, including AppProjects that never configured destinationServiceAccounts and therefore silently move to whatever the destination namespace's default service account can do.

Nothing on the hydrated branch records who pushed a commit. The hydrator design copies commitAuthor forward from the dry commit into the README and hydrator.metadata, and every push is made by the GitHub App credential in the repository-write Secret, never by the person named in that field; the signing feature that would tie a commit to a key defaults to commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits false. So a holder of the repository-write credential can push a hydrated commit attributed in metadata to any dry-commit author, and the evidence a reviewer would consult (git history plus hydrator.metadata) reproduces the attacker's chosen attribution rather than contradicting it. Detection of such a push depends on an opt-in that is off by default.

The History and Rollback design pushes to the sync branch outside the commit server, and the commit server is the only component that holds the signing key, mounted from the Secret in the Argo CD namespace. The consequence is that the check actually deciding whether a rollback lands is the git host enforcing the branch's SourceIntegrity policy, not Argo CD: the rollback push is unsigned and is rejected there, while the UI shows only a failed push with no messaging tying it back to signing and no retry path. Where SourceIntegrity is not configured on the sync branch, the same reasoning removes the only enforcement, and any holder of write access to that branch can place manifests on it that Argo CD will sync with no commit-server record of the push.

The CI diff failures reporting that user system:serviceaccount:argocd:argocd-server is attempting to grant RBAC permissions not currently held are the Kubernetes escalation-prevention check firing against the identity performing the server-side apply dry-run, and they appeared in projects that had just enabled the sync impersonation flag. The impersonation design routes the sync operation through the AppProject's destinationServiceAccounts while leaving the diff path on its own identity, so the identity the check is evaluated against on the diff surface is not the identity that performs the actual apply. A ClusterRole the diff surface reports as forbidden can still be applied by the sync path when the mapped service account holds those grants, which means the diff output is not evidence of what the sync is authorized to do, in either direction.
